          "text": "## 2.2 Experimental method\nGlycine solutions of different concentrations were used as leaching agents, in which Gly− is the ligand. Hydrogen peroxide (30%) was used as a reducing agent. All the chemical reagents used in this study were analytically pure, and the solutions were prepared using distilled water at the prescribed concentrations.\nAs required by the experiment, a glycine solution at a specific concentration was made. The solution was warmed up in a water bath with a constant temperature while being stirred with a magnetic stirrer. Once the desired temperature was reached, solid NaOH pellets were added to the solution until the experimentally set pH value was achieved, which was monitored using a pH meter. After the solution reached the required values and stabilized at the specified temperature, 20 g of spent LIBs powder was added, and the reaction was timed. After the reaction time, the beaker was removed and left to cool to room temperature. Then, the leachate and leach residue were separated by vacuum filtration, and the metal content of the leach solution was measured. It was worth mentioning that experiments with reaction temperatures exceeding 100 °C needed to be carried out in a highpressure reactor. Due to the mixing of leaching and washing solutions, all concentrations of impurity metals in this paper were converted to concentrations in 100 mL of solution.",

For instance, the extraction ratio of Li increases from 26.51% to 94.13% as the temperature is increased from 50 to 90 ℃.\nWith the increase in temperature, the reaction rate is accelerated by the rise of molecular diffusion ability, and the complexation of Gly− is improved. Thus, the efficiency of leaching for each metal is significantly enhanced. Subsequently, the leaching efficiency of each metal gradually leveled off by continuing to raise the temperature. The temperature can affect the complexation ability between Gly− and M2+ (M=Co, Ni, Mn), as well as the difficult degree of metal ions and OH− forming hydroxide or oxide precipitates. As a result, the leaching efficiency exhibits the zig-zag phenomenon. Considering that in addition to the increase in the leaching efficiency of the valuable metals, the dissolution of the impurity metals will also be enhanced to some extent, as shown in Table S2.           "text": "## 3.1.3 Effect of leaching agent concentration\nThe aim was to investigate the recovery of Li, Co, Ni, and Mn from spent LIBs powder over leaching agent concentration and the dissolution of impurities in the leach solution. The experiments were conducted under the following conditions: leaching time 3 h, leaching temperature 90 ℃, L/S 5 mL:1 g, pH 8, and stirring speed 400 r/min.\nIt can be found from Figure 4(c) that properly enhancing the [Gly−]T concentration plays a favorable role in improving the leaching efficiency of valuable metals from spent LIBs powder. The overall leaching efficiency of the reaction system tends to increase as the [Gly−]T concentration increases from 0.5 mol/L to 3.0 mol/L. With the increases of the ligand concentration, the free Gly in the system increases and forms more complexes with the metal ions. Moreover, the leaching efficiency of Co decreases to some extent while the concentration of Gly− increases from 1 to 2.5 mol/L. In this concentration range, the coordination reaction of Ni with Gly− has a higher priority relative to Co, resulting in the preferential coordination of Gly− with Ni.\nAs the ligand concentration gradually increases to 3.0 mol/L, the ligand reactivity increases, and many stable metal complexes are formed in the solution. When the ligand concentration is more significant than 3.0 mol/L, the coordination effect between Gly− and the metals in the spent LIBs powder gradually is saturated, the overall viscosity in the solution is increased, and the motility of each metal ion is decreased, resulting in the leaching efficiency starting to decline.\nAt the same time, too high a concentration of ligands will cause the reaction products to adhere to the surface of the leaching material, affecting the leaching reaction positively. When the leaching solution gradually becomes supersaturated, the overall coordination ability of the glycinate is reduced. In general, as [Gly−]T increases, coordination ions with different coordination numbers are formed, and between these complex ion conversions, leaching efficiency will experience fluctuations. The leaching efficiency curves obtain the best leaching results for Li, Ni, Co, and Mn at a leaching agent concentration of 3.0 mol/L, with 45.31%, 57.35%, 28.63%, and 15.31%, respectively.           "text": "## 3.2 Leaching kinetics\nMixing control:\nln(1 - x) / 3 + (1 - x) ^(- 1 / 3) - 1 = k3 t (Eq. 4)\nIn the above equation, x represents the leaching efficiencies of Li, Co, Ni, and Mn; k1-3 ^ (min ^-1) represents the integrated rate constants; t (min) represents the leaching time.\nThe experiments were performed in a 1.5 L beaker. The beaker was filled with 1 L of 3 mol/Lsolution of [ Gly ^- ]T, and the pH was adjusted to 8 with NaOH solid particles at 25, 35, 45, 55, and 65 ^∘C. 200 g of spent LIBs powder was added. The leaching efficiency of the target metals was then analyzed by sampling every 10 min. It was found that the early leaching rate of lithium was too fast, so the sampling interval for lithium was every minute in the first 10 min of the reaction start and every five minutes after 10 min. The results of the Li, Co, Ni, and Mn leaching efficiencies are shown in Figure 8.\nThe experimental data in Figure 8 were fitted, and the results obtained from the fitting are shown in Figure 9 and Table 2. In addition, the Arrhenius equation [46] is applied to plot lnk against 1000/T, thus calculating the activation energy of the target metal and determining the type of reaction.\nlnk = lnA - Ea / R T (Eq. 5) where Ea is the apparent activation energy; A is the frequency factor; T (K) is the leaching temperature; and R is the gas constant 8.3145 J/(K·mol).\nThe correlation results of the activation energy fit are shown in Figure 10. The leaching activation energies of Li, Ni, Co, and Mn are 45.73, 53.13, 50.64, and 60.36 kJ/mol, respectively. They indicated that the leaching process is controlled by chemical reactions. The leaching temperature has a significant influence on the leaching efficiencies of metals. Based on the magnitude of activation energy, Li is more easily leached, and Mn is the most difficult to be leached. This is also verified in the condition experiment.\nThe Arrhenius equations for Li, Co, Ni, and Mn in the temperature range of 25 to 65 ^∘C can be derived from the fitting results of Figure 10.",
